title: Testing Distributed Systems
subtitle: Watch one Orders service get tested with five kinds of test, from unit tests to load tests, and see what each layer catches.
learn: Why a test pyramid keeps most tests fast and few tests broad
How contract tests catch API drift between teams without a shared staging environment
Why integration tests should use a real database, not a mock
How to inject latency and failures to prove timeouts and fallbacks work
How a load test finds limits such as connection pool exhaustion

steps.title: Green tests, broken checkout
steps.body: Imagine the Orders service has hundreds of passing unit tests. Yet after a release, checkout breaks because the Payments team renamed a JSON field. Later, one slow Payments reply freezes the whole service. Unit tests could not see either problem, because they fake everything outside the code. Real failures happen in the gaps between components, so we need tests for those gaps too.
steps.idea: Passing unit tests prove your code matches your assumptions, not that your assumptions are true.
steps.caption: Orders talks to a database and to Payments. Those links are where bugs hide.

steps.title: Many fast unit tests
steps.body: The bottom layer is unit tests: tiny checks of pure logic, like adding up a price or moving an order from new to paid. They run in memory with no network. The runner sends 1,200 of them to Orders. At about 5 ms each that is only a few seconds, plus about 30 s to build and start up, so roughly 40 seconds in total. They are cheap, so run them on every commit. Above them sit fewer, slower layers, and at the very top a handful of end-to-end tests that drive the whole system through its UI or API. Those are realistic but slow and flaky (they sometimes fail for no code reason). This shape is the test pyramid, a rule of thumb: the higher the layer, the slower and costlier, so keep fewer.
steps.idea: Put most tests where feedback is fastest and failures are easiest to diagnose.
steps.caption: The runner sends 1,200 in-memory unit tests to Orders; all pass in about 40 s.

steps.title: Contract tests for the API gap
steps.body: Orders is the consumer of the Payments API (it calls it). Payments is the provider (it serves it). Orders' tests write down what it relies on, such as 'POST /charges replies with amount and status', and publish that contract to a broker, a shared noticeboard for contracts. Payments' own build then downloads the contracts and checks its real code against them. If Payments renames status, its build fails before release, so the team that caused the break sees it first. Say 40 contract tests add about 15 seconds. No shared staging environment is needed.
steps.idea: A contract test catches breaking API changes at the provider's build, where they are cheapest to fix.
steps.caption: Orders publishes its contract; Payments fetches it, verifies, and reports back.

steps.title: Use the real database
steps.body: Integration tests use real dependencies instead of fakes. The runner starts a throwaway Postgres in a container (tools like Testcontainers do this), applies the real migrations (the scripts that create the tables), and runs 80 tests that send real SQL. A fake database would happily accept a query that breaks a unique rule, misspells a column, or needs a migration you forgot to write. A real one rejects it. In the animation, Orders inserts an order and the database answers. These tests take about three minutes, so run them on every pull request, not every keystroke.
steps.idea: Stub remote services you do not control; run the infrastructure you own, such as your database, for real.
steps.caption: Orders runs real SQL against a Postgres container; the database enforces its rules.

steps.title: Inject latency and failures
steps.body: Here Payments is a stub (a fake that returns canned replies) behind a fault proxy, a middleman that can delay, drop or break calls on command. The contract test from step 3 keeps the stub honest. The test makes Payments take 5 seconds. Orders must give up after its own 2 s timeout and reply 'payment pending, we will confirm shortly' instead of hanging. A second test retries with the same idempotency key (an ID that stops duplicate charges) and checks the customer is charged once. Untested timeout code is probably wrong. Say 15 fault tests add about 30 seconds. Other faults to try: connection reset, HTTP 503, duplicate delivery.
steps.idea: Failure-handling code only works if you have watched it run against a failure.
steps.caption: The proxy stalls Payments for 5 s; Orders must stop waiting at 2 s.

steps.title: Load test the baseline
steps.body: A load test shows how the system behaves when many users arrive at once. The load generator replays realistic traffic, say 500 requests per second for 10 minutes, against a production-like copy of the system. It reports latency percentiles, not averages. p99 means 99 percent of requests were faster, and the slowest 1 percent is what users complain about. The healthy result here is p99 near 180 ms with errors below 0.1 percent. Save it as the baseline to compare against after every release.
steps.idea: Load tests produce a baseline; their value is comparing against it later.
steps.caption: 500 req/s flow through Orders and Postgres; p99 is 180 ms and errors are tiny.

steps.title: Push past the limit
steps.body: Now raise the rate to 1,500 requests per second. Assume each request holds a database connection for about 20 ms and the service keeps a pool of 20 (a fixed set of reusable connections). Each connection serves about 50 requests per second, so the pool handles about 1,000 req/s. The extra third waits in line until the 2.5 s client timeout. So p99 reaches about 2.5 seconds and about 33 percent of requests fail. No unit test shows this, because the limit comes from many requests competing at once. Fixes: faster queries, a pooler such as PgBouncer, a cache, or shedding load early. A bigger pool alone often just moves the queue to the database.
steps.idea: Load tests find the knee in the curve where queues build and latency explodes.
steps.caption: At 1,500 req/s the pool runs out: p99 is about 2.5 s and a third of requests fail.

steps.title: Cost and flakiness
steps.body: Broad tests are expensive and can fail for reasons unrelated to your change, such as a slow CI machine, a shared environment, or a timing race. A suite that fails randomly teaches people to rerun it and ignore red results. So keep the upper layers few and give each a clear purpose. Make tests deterministic (same result every run) with fixed random seeds and no real sleeps, and quarantine flaky tests quickly. Production monitoring and gradual rollouts, covered in other lessons, catch what testing cannot.
steps.idea: A test suite is only useful if people trust a red result.
steps.caption: Each layer adds coverage and also cost; flaky tests wear down trust.

steps.title: Which layer catches what
steps.body: Five kinds of test, each aimed at a different risk. Unit tests guard logic. Contract tests guard API agreements between teams. Integration tests with real dependencies guard SQL and wiring. Fault injection guards timeouts and fallbacks. Load tests guard capacity. Keep many cheap tests at the bottom and a few expensive ones on top. Each layer answers a different question, so skipping one leaves that question unanswered.
steps.idea: Match each risk to the cheapest test that can reveal it.
steps.caption: Five kinds of test, five different risks covered.

quiz.q: The Payments team renames a response field. Which test would fail in the Payments build before release?
options: A unit test inside Orders
A load test against Orders
A provider verification of Orders' published contract
A snapshot of the Orders database
quiz.why: The broker holds what Orders relies on. Payments verifies its real code against that contract, so the rename fails their build.

quiz.q: Why run integration tests against a real Postgres container instead of a mocked repository?
options: A real database enforces constraints, types and SQL syntax that a mock silently accepts
Mocks cannot be written for databases
Containers make tests run faster than unit tests
It removes the need for unit tests
quiz.why: A mock returns whatever you told it to, so bugs in the SQL or schema stay hidden. A real database rejects them.

quiz.q: A load test reports an average latency of 90 ms, yet users complain about slow checkouts. What should you check?
options: Only the maximum single request
The number of unit tests
Whether the load generator is a container
p95 and p99 percentiles, which show the slow tail
quiz.why: Averages hide the slow tail. A few percent of very slow requests barely move the mean but affect many real users.

quiz.q: A fault-injection test makes a dependency take 5 s, and Orders also hangs for 5 s. What does this reveal?
options: The dependency is healthy
The timeout is missing or misconfigured
The test pyramid is inverted
The contract is out of date
quiz.why: A correct client would stop waiting at its own timeout. Hanging for the full delay shows that protection is not working.

quiz.q: Your suite has few unit tests and thousands of browser-driven end-to-end tests, and it fails randomly. What is the best direction?
options: Add more end-to-end tests
Rerun failures until they pass
Move checks down to unit, contract and integration tests, and keep few end-to-end ones
Delete the integration tests
quiz.why: Lower layers are faster and more deterministic. Shifting coverage down gives quicker, more trustworthy feedback.

cheatsheet.def: Rule of thumb: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests. Cost and flakiness rise with each layer.
Checks that a consumer's expectations of an API match what the provider actually returns, verified in the provider's build.
Start real dependencies such as Postgres or Kafka in disposable containers for each test run, then throw them away.
A stand-in (stub, mock, fake) for a dependency. Use for remote services you do not control or that are slow; run infrastructure you own, such as your database, for real.
Load test: expected traffic, to confirm the baseline. Stress test: push beyond it to find the breaking point.
p99 means 99 percent of requests were faster. Report percentiles, not averages, because users feel the tail.
Deliberately add delay, errors, drops or duplicates to a dependency to prove timeouts, retries and fallbacks behave.
A test that passes and fails without code changes. Fix or quarantine it fast; it erodes trust in the whole suite.
